lead: A leaf (laminated) spring is a stack of flat steel strips of graded length, clamped at the centre and fixed to the vehicle frame at the ends. It works as a beam in bending, and because the number of leaves falls towards the ends roughly as the bending moment falls, every leaf is stressed about equally. The spring carries the load, locates the axle and damps vibration by friction between the leaves. Trucks, buses, trailers and railway wagons use it.
prereq: You need bending stress M/Z and beam deflection from the chapters on stresses, and spring energy from helical compression springs.

blocks.text: The longest leaf, the master leaf, is rolled into an eye at each end for the shackle pins. Some springs have one or two more full-length leaves under it. The shorter graduated leaves lie below. A centre bolt and U-bolts clamp the stack to the axle, and rebound clips keep the leaves together when the spring springs back.

A semi-elliptic spring of eye-to-eye span 2L₁ with central load 2W acts as two cantilevers of length L, each loaded by W at its eye. Bending moment grows linearly from the eye to the centre. A triangular plate of constant thickness has a section modulus that grows the same way, so its stress is the same everywhere: a beam of uniform strength. Cut that triangle into strips and stack them, and you have the graduated leaves.
The clamped centre does not bend, so the effective length is 2L = 2L₁ − l, where l is the width of the centre band (about two-thirds of the U-bolt spacing when U-bolts are used).

With n<sub>f</sub> full-length leaves (including the master leaf), n<sub>g</sub> graduated leaves, n = n<sub>f</sub> + n<sub>g</sub>, leaf width b and thickness t, the full-length leaves are stressed 50 % more than the graduated ones:
σ<sub>f</sub> is the stress in the full-length leaves; the graduated leaves carry σ<sub>g</sub> = 12WL/[bt²(3n<sub>f</sub> + 2n<sub>g</sub>)].

δ is the deflection at the eye relative to the centre, in mm; E the Young's modulus, about 207 000 MPa for spring steel. With all leaves graduated (n<sub>f</sub> = 0) this becomes 6WL³/(Enbt³); with all full-length, 4WL³/(Enbt³).

To stress all leaves equally, the full-length leaves are given a slightly larger radius of curvature than the graduated leaves. Before assembly a gap C, the nip, appears between them at the ends. Tightening the centre bolt closes it, which pre-stresses the full-length leaves in the opposite sense to the load and the graduated leaves in the same sense. Under the full load all leaves then reach the same stress:

blocks.where: σ is the equal stress in every leaf after nipping. The nip is C = 2WL³/(Enbt³), and the initial load on the centre bolt is P<sub>i</sub> = 2n<sub>f</sub>n<sub>g</sub>W/[n(3n<sub>f</sub> + 2n<sub>g</sub>)].

blocks.text: Nipping lowers the peak stress in the master leaf, which carries the eyes and is the most important leaf. The deflection formula is unchanged. Design steps: choose b and t from standard strip sizes (b is often 6 to 12 times t), find n for the permissible stress, check deflection, find the nip and bolt load, and check the eye and shackle pin.

examples.question: A semi-elliptic leaf spring has an eye-to-eye span of 1000 mm and a central band 100 mm wide. It carries a central load of 9 kN. It has 2 full-length leaves and 6 graduated leaves, each 75 mm wide and 10 mm thick; E = 207 000 MPa. Find the stresses without and with nipping, the deflection, the nip and the bolt load.
steps: Effective length 2L = 1000 − 100 = 900 mm, so L = 450 mm. Load at each eye W = 9000/2 = 4500 N.
With nipping: σ = 6 × 4500 × 450/(8 × 7500) = 202.5 MPa in every leaf.
examples.answer: 270 MPa (full-length) and 180 MPa (graduated) without nip; 202.5 MPa in all leaves with a 6.6 mm nip and a 750 N bolt load; deflection 17.6 mm.

traps: Using the whole eye-to-eye span as L. L is half the effective length, after subtracting the clamped band: 450 mm here, not 1000 or 500 mm.
Using the central load 2W as W. Every formula uses the load at one eye.
Leaving out the master leaf from n<sub>f</sub>. The master leaf is a full-length leaf.
Thinking nipping changes the deflection. It only redistributes the stress between leaves.
Mixing GPa and MPa: with N and mm, E must be in MPa (207 000).

quiz.q: What is the master leaf, and why does it need the lowest stress?
quiz.a: The longest leaf, rolled into eyes at both ends. It carries the shackle loads and locates the axle, so its failure drops the vehicle; nipping lowers its stress.
Giving the full-length leaves a larger radius of curvature than the graduated leaves, so that clamping pre-stresses them and all leaves reach equal stress under full load.

quiz.q: Why is a leaf spring called a beam of uniform strength?
quiz.a: The graduated leaves stop where the bending moment is small, so the section modulus falls towards the eyes in step with the moment and the bending stress is nearly the same along the length.

quiz.q: A spring with 6 graduated leaves only, 60 mm × 6 mm, carries 2 kN at each eye with L = 400 mm. Find σ and δ (E = 207 000 MPa).
Find the nip and bolt load for n<sub>f</sub> = 1, n<sub>g</sub> = 7, W = 3 kN, L = 500 mm, b = 60 mm, t = 8 mm, E = 207 000 MPa.
If the leaf thickness is doubled with everything else fixed, what happens to stress and deflection?
quiz.a: Stress ∝ 1/t², so it falls to a quarter; deflection ∝ 1/t³, so it falls to an eighth. The spring becomes far stiffer, which is why thickness is chosen with care.

beyond: Not for the exam. Parabolic leaf springs use a few leaves that are rolled thinner towards the ends, so each leaf is a uniform-strength beam and inter-leaf friction is small. Glass-fibre composite leaf springs are lighter and do not rust. Search for parabolic leaf spring and composite leaf spring.

figure.caption: The worked example’s spring: 1000 mm between eyes, a 100 mm centre band, so each cantilever is L = 450 mm with 4.5 kN at the eye. Two full-length and six graduated leaves 75 × 10 mm; nipping evens the leaf stresses from 270 and 180 MPa to 202.5 MPa.
